SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · HOW LLMS WORK
7
UNDER THE HOOD
A prediction engine, sent to finishing school
1 · Pretraining
Months, trillions of words: learn to predict the next token on internet-scale text. Language, facts, and reasoning patterns compress into billions of learned weights.
2 · Instruction tuning
Curated example dialogues teach it to follow instructions and answer questions — instead of just continuing your text.
3 · Human feedback (RLHF)
People rank outputs; the model is tuned toward helpful, honest, harmless. And it never stops: your thumbs-up today is preference data for the NEXT model.
Knowledge is frozen at the cutoff — with escape hatches. 
Training ends months before release. Many assistants compensate: live web search pulls today’s pages into the prompt; RAG (concept 3) plugs in your own documents.
Why prompting exists: 
the model completes your text — the prompt is the only steering wheel you have. A complete prompt doesn’t make the model smarter: it deletes wrong guesses.
PROMPT 2/7
Narrowing the guesses — two separate sends
STEP 1 · TYPE THIS → “Finish this sentence 5 different ways: We should move the launch date because”
WHY → no facts yet — watch it scatter across guesses.
STEP 2 · TYPE THIS → “Now 5 more ways, knowing: B2B software firm, competitor launches May 3, our beta ends April 20.”
WHY → your facts didn’t make it smarter — they deleted wrong guesses.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX2-Guesses of your Course Workbook

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Title metaphor first: “a prediction engine, sent to finishing school.”
2) Three cards LEFT TO RIGHT — pretraining, instruction tuning, human feedback. On card 3, land the after-ship line: RLHF never really stops — every thumbs-up/down you click, and on personal accounts your chats themselves, become the preference data that trains the next model. (That is exactly what “trains on your data by default” means on the trust slide in Part 2.)
3) LEFT callout: the cutoff — AND its two escape hatches: live web search, and RAG for your own documents.
4) RIGHT callout, slowly — the thesis of the course: the prompt is the only steering wheel; a complete prompt DELETES WRONG GUESSES.

TRY IT — PROMPT 2/7 (two sends; copy from tab EX2-Guesses)
Send 1 scatters: budget, staffing, quality. Send 2 orbits May 3 and April 20.
Debrief line: “Grade the directions, not the sentences.”

BRIDGE —
“Six concepts, quick — starting with what the model actually reads.”

ACRONYMS —
RLHF = Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — card 3.
RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation — concept 3, shortly.

CONTENT —
InstructGPT fact worth telling: raters preferred a well-tuned 1.3B model over raw 175B GPT-3 — tuning beat 100× scale.
v1.6: cutoff callout gains the web-search/RAG escape hatches; RLHF card gains the after-ship story (owner request).
ART — the corner graduation robot is an owner-generated illustration (R16): the “finishing school” of the subtitle, literally.

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
9
CONCEPT 2 · CONTEXT WINDOW
A desk, not a filing cabinet
The context window is working memory for one conversation: your question, the system prompt, chat history, attached files, and search results must all fit on the desk.
Close the chat and the desk is swept clean. Nothing persists unless a memory feature or a saved file re-loads it.
By 2026, ~1M tokens (≈750,000 words) is the flagship standard. Consumer apps often enforce smaller limits than the raw model.
In very long chats the middle gets skimmed — accuracy is highest at the start and the end (“lost in the middle”).
What’s on the desk right now
System prompt & instructions
Every prior turn — both sides
Attached documents
Tool & search results
Habits that exploit the desk: 
① long documents at the TOP, question at the END (up to ~30% better answers) · ② label multiple documents · ③ new topic → new chat · ④ long thread → run the handoff move below.
A desk with a filing cabinet? Persistent files, notes and standing instructions are what agentic tools bolt onto the desk — Part 5. Pros call this CONTEXT ENGINEERING: the prompt is the briefing; context is everything on the desk — even what nobody typed.
PROMPT 4/7
The desk — explained, then carried
STEP 1 · TYPE THIS → “Explain your context window like I’m a 5th grader: the desk, what fits on it, and what happens when I close this chat. Under 100 words.”
WHY → the AI describes its own working memory, plainly.
STEP 2 · TYPE THIS → (homework) “Summarize our chat so far in under 80 words, titled HANDOFF.”
WHY → tonight, paste into a fresh chat, ask “where was I?” — it picks up your course.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX4-Handoff of your Course Workbook

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) The analogy first: “a desk, not a filing cabinet.”
2) Left bullets; on the bold one, draw the U-shape in the air — attention high at the start, sags in the middle, high at the end.
3) Right card: the four things on the desk right now.
4) Teal card: the four habits — habit ④ is about to be performed.
5) Amber card: one sentence — the filing-cabinet teaser for Part 5. Plant the seed, move on.

TRY IT — PROMPT 4/7 (copy from tab EX4-Handoff)
Step 1 in class; step 2 is homework in the same thread.
Recovery (someone’s fresh chat knows unpasted things): “your tool has a filing cabinet bolted to the desk — hold that thought for Part 5.”

BRIDGE —
“And what if what you need was never on the desk? RAG.”

ACRONYMS —
1M = one million tokens.

CONTENT —
“Lost in the middle” = Liu et al. 2023 (TACL). The up-to-~30% figure is Anthropic’s own long-context guidance.
1M-token flagship standard verified Aug 2026 across Claude, GPT-5.x, Gemini, and the Chinese open-weight flagships.

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
10
CONCEPT 3 · RAG
An open-book exam — audit the librarian
The problem RAG solves: the model’s knowledge is frozen and public; your work runs on private documents it has never seen — and must never be trained on.
1 · Ask
Plain question: “What does the supplier agreement say about re-inspection?”
2 · Retrieve
Semantic search finds the most relevant passages — by meaning, not keywords.
3 · Augment
Those passages are placed on the model’s desk, behind the scenes.
4 · Generate
The model answers from the supplied text — and cites where it looked.
Why enterprises build on it: 
current (re-index in minutes, no retraining) · checkable (citations to the exact passage) · private (retrieval feeds one answer, teaches the model nothing) · access-aware.
The failure mode to respect: 
fetch the wrong page — an outdated revision, a near-miss document — and the model still writes a fluent, confident, CITED answer from it. Check the citation, not just the prose.
You already use this. Our internal company assistant — the one where you upload documentation and “talk” to it — is RAG in production. Every step on this slide happens each time you ask it a question.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Expand the acronym ONCE, then the analogy: an open-book exam — a librarian fetches pages from YOUR documents; the student writes from those pages.
2) Four step cards LEFT TO RIGHT.
3) Green card: current, checkable, private, access-aware.
4) Red card, slowly: wrong page → fluent, confident, CITED, wrong. “Check the citation, not the prose.”
5) Teal band: “you’ve been running this loop all along” — keep it generic, no product names.

BRIDGE —
“When do you prompt, when do you retrieve, when do you fine-tune? The escalation ladder.”

ACRONYMS —
RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

CONTENT —
Retrieval ≠ training is the privacy point to repeat.
This is the engine behind internal document assistants and Copilot-over-SharePoint.
ART — the open-book-exam scene (robot writing from the book, librarian delivering a glowing page) is an owner-generated illustration (R16); gesture at it when you say the analogy.

notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 3 · THE ANATOMY
21
THE UNIVERSAL ANATOMY
Seven parts, one body — what good looks like
ROLE
“You are a precise editor. You add no facts that are not in the source.”
TASK
“Summarize the attached Q2 returns report for the operations lead.”
CONTEXT
“We’re a mid-size electronics manufacturer. Return rate = returns ÷ shipped. The export has a totals row — exclude it.”
FORMAT
“≤ 150 words: the headline number first, then three bullets.”
EXAMPLES
<example> March’s summary — the one the team liked </example>
THE OUT
“Anything the report doesn’t state: write UNKNOWN — never estimate. List the gaps at the end.”
THE STOP
“Deliver the summary, then stop — nothing beyond.”
Note the industry line: what business you’re in is CONTEXT — name your world; never assume it knows.
The Out, defined: the escape route for missing information — name the honest move (write UNKNOWN · never estimate · list the gaps), so the model never has to choose between obeying you and being honest.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Frame: “one prompt, seven parts — and the parts make a BODY. Everything in Part 3 is refinements of this picture.”
2) Walk the FIGURE (owner-generated art) top to bottom, naming each organ: the head thinks in the right posture (Role) · the heart is why it beats at all (Task) · the bloodstream feeds every organ (Context) · the skeleton holds the shape (Format) · the hands show how it’s done (Examples) · the immune system rejects invented facts (the Out) · the skin is where the ACTION ends (the Stop — perform exactly the named action, then stop). Then the caption: miss an organ and it still walks — it just fails in a predictable way. That predictability is the diagnosis grid (tab EX-Report). (The image caption says the Stop is “where the job ends” — SAY it the owner’s way: where the ACTION ends.)
3) RIGHT card: the same body written out — read it top to bottom as ONE continuous prompt (~90 words, under two minutes to write).
4) SLOW on THE OUT row — the element people define worst, so define it fully: the Out is the ESCAPE ROUTE you write for missing information. It has three parts, all visible in the example: the CONDITION (“anything the report doesn’t state”), the HONEST MOVE (“write UNKNOWN — never estimate”), and the SURFACING (“list the gaps at the end” — so the gaps reach YOU instead of hiding). Then the why, in one sentence: a model is trained to always produce an answer — if you don’t specify the honest move, INVENTING is the only way it can obey your prompt. “Say so” alone is weaker: it names no form; UNKNOWN + a gap list is checkable in the output.
5) The amber line — owner-requested and worth saying twice: YOUR INDUSTRY IS CONTEXT. “We’re a mid-size electronics manufacturer” changes every answer downstream; people constantly assume the AI knows their world. It doesn’t until you say so.
6) Teal band: read the Out definition verbatim — it is the slide’s one formal definition.

BRIDGE —
“Now each element properly — and what each one BUYS you.”

ACRONYMS —
Q2 = second quarter. XML-style tags = the angle-bracket fences around examples.

CONTENT —
v1.6: rebuilt around the body figure (owner: “let’s see how creative and artistic you can get”); the vendor-recipe panel moved off-slide (owner request) — keep in reserve for questions: Anthropic (role · clear task · context · format · examples), OpenAI (role & instructions · context · format · few-shot), Google (Persona·Task·Context·Format), Microsoft (Goal·Context·Source·Expectations) — four official guides, one anatomy: convergence, not our opinion.
The 21-words stat (moved off-slide in v1.10 to make room for the Out definition; say it if useful): Google’s Oct 2024 Workspace guide found the most fruitful prompts averaged ~21 words with context — most people type fewer than nine (directional, not gospel).
v1.10 (owner request): the Out re-defined and its example upgraded — condition + honest move + surfacing (“anything the report doesn’t state: write UNKNOWN — never estimate; list the gaps at the end”), with the formal definition in the teal band. The same sharpened definition is on the element card (3 of 3), the cheat sheet, and tab EX-Report.
Anthropic’s golden rule belongs in the room: show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context — if they’d be confused, the model will be too.
If the cold open was used: this slide is its debrief — the vague line is the returns-data prompt with every element filled in.
21

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 3 · THE ELEMENTS
22
THE ELEMENTS · WHAT EACH BUYS YOU — 1 OF 3
Role & Task: the posture, and the question
Role
who is answering — decompose it into personality statements: testable behaviors, not titles
What you get — the right altitude and posture: an expert stance you can hold it to, line by line — and a consistent voice readers can feel.
Why — a role won’t make the model smarter — two studies (162 personas; a 2025 six-model replication) found zero accuracy gain — but it reliably reshapes voice and register. The craft is writing the RIGHT requirements: each personality statement is checkable in the output; a title is a vibe it can fake. (Zheng 2024 · Wharton 2025 · PersonaLLM 2024)
weak   “You are a senior analyst.”
strong “You never invent numbers; you state n; you say what the data can’t answer.”
weak   “You are a helpful assistant.”
strong “You challenge weak assumptions instead of agreeing; you flag uncertainty rather than smooth it over.”
Task
verb + object + audience + success criterion — and the SEQUENCE, when order matters
What you get — an answer to YOUR question, sized for its audience — and a model that knows when it is done.

Context & Format: the facts, and the contract
Context
what the model cannot know on its own
What you get — answers that are right for US — your definitions, your quirks, your constraints — instead of generically right.
Why — the model fills every gap with the most plausible guess; context deletes wrong guesses (Part 1’s launch-date drill). Measured: answer-from-the-supplied-text instructions cut memory-override errors 35%→3% and lifted accuracy on unanswerable questions 31%→88%. Flip side: it trusts your context even when it’s wrong — quality is on you. (Zhou 2023 · Omar 2025)
weak   “Use our standard definitions.”
strong “Return rate = returns ÷ shipped. Quirk: the export has a totals row — exclude it and say so.”
weak   “You know our business.”
strong “We’re a mid-size electronics manufacturer; ‘returns’ means warranty returns, not cancelled orders.”
Format
the output contract — shape, cap, tone
What you get — output you can use as-is: right shape, right length, no reformatting pass — and answers you can compare across runs.
Why — a numeric cap is enforceable; “short and professional” is a mood the model interprets freely. Spelling out structure is nearly free reliability — schema-enforced output went from under 40% to 100% compliant. (OpenAI 2024 · JSONSchemaBench 2025)
weak   “Keep it short and professional.”
strong “≤ 120 words: the ask in sentence one, two facts with numbers, the deadline.”
weak   “Make it a nice table.”
strong “A table with exactly: Site | Return rate | vs target | Trend — one row per site, worst first.”

3) Format — land “a numeric cap is enforceable; an adjective is a mood.” The myth to kill: “JSON makes models dumber” — the follow-up studies showed well-built format constraints cost nothing and often help.

THE ELEMENTS · WHAT EACH BUYS YOU — 3 OF 3
Examples — and the two one-sentence safety valves
Examples
3–5 diverse demonstrations, edge case included
What you get — work that matches the standard in your head — including how the hard cases get handled.
Why — the model imitates what it sees: examples teach format and style; on modern tuned models they steer shape more than facts. Include one edge case — it copies your edge-case handling too. (Brown 2020 · Min 2022)
weak   three clones of the happy case
strong one typical + one edge + one reject case, clearly separated
weak   “Write it like the good ones.”
strong “Match this: [March’s summary] — same tone, same length. Here’s one we rejected, and why.”
The Out
the escape route for missing information — condition · honest move · surfacing
What you get — an honest UNKNOWN with the gaps listed — instead of an invented answer.
Why — a model is trained to always produce an answer; unless you specify the honest move, inventing is the only way to obey you. One sentence of permission cut hallucinations on planted-error questions from 53% to 23% (GPT-4o) — and under 8% on GPT-5. (Omar 2025 · OpenAI 2025)
weak   “Do not hallucinate.” (bare bans backfire)
strong “Anything the document doesn’t state: write UNKNOWN — never estimate. List the gaps at the end.”
The Stop
the action to perform — and its boundary
What you get — bounded work that ends where you said — not ten charts and no answer.
Why — converts open-ended capability into a scoped job with a finish line. In Part 5 it grows up to become gates and autonomy rules for agents.
weak   “Keep it focused.”
strong “Answer these three questions, then stop — do not go exploring.”
Seven elements — each moves something out of your head onto the page; when output disappoints, one stayed in your head.

3) The Stop: one sentence converts open-ended capability into a bounded job; file it away — it becomes agent gates in Part 5.
4) Footer, verbatim — it is the unifying idea: every element moves something out of your head onto the page.

THE TOOLKIT · PLAN · DO · CHECK · ACT
The toolkit is a loop
P
PLAN — draft the ask
· The anatomy: all seven elements, filled
· Be specific — and say WHY behind each rule
· Separate your ask from the pasted material
· Show 2–3 examples, one edge case included
delegate it → “I need [X] for [audience], with [constraints]. Draft me a strong prompt, then wait.”
D
DO — run it, in order
· Number the steps — order stated is order followed
· Add “wait for my OK” where you want control
· Documents on top, ask at the end · fresh chat per topic
delegate it → “1) Outline only. 2) Wait for my OK. 3) Draft section by section.”
C
CHECK — inspect before you trust
· Name the failed element — the symptom→element grid, tab EX-Report
· Self-check on NAMED criteria — never “are you sure?”
· Blind review: paste it as “a colleague’s draft”
· Numbers reconcile to a known total · citations + the out
delegate it → “Verify against these three criteria and list exactly what fails.”
A
ACT — refine, then standardize
· Fix ONE element, rerun — never reword at random
· Metaprompt: have the AI rewrite the prompt itself
· Works twice? Name it, version it, library (Part 6)
· Re-baseline on every model upgrade
delegate it → “Rewrite this prompt so it more consistently produces X.”
This is PDCA — the Deming/Toyota improvement cycle, applied to prompts. The Lean Enterprise Institute now teaches “Prompt-Do-Check-Act.” Every phase is delegable — the white lines show how; the methods keep you in charge.
W. EDWARDS DEMING · 1900–1993

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) The frame is the owner’s design — say it plainly: “there is no separate list of techniques. The toolkit IS the improvement loop you already know from the factory floor: Plan, Do, Check, Act — with the right prompting method for each phase.” In practice the four phases are simply: draft → inspect → refine → standardize.
2) Walk the four quadrants P → D → C → A. Per quadrant: read the methods fast, then the WHITE LINE slowly — it is the copy-paste move, and it is also the delegation move: planning can be delegated (the AI drafts the prompt), checking can be delegated (against YOUR named criteria), acting can be delegated (metaprompt). You keep judgment; it does the labor.
3) CHECK is the quadrant to slow on — four different verification methods, one per failure type: wrong element → the grid; quality → named criteria; bias → blind review; numbers → reconcile to an anchor. “Are you sure?” appears in none of them, on purpose (the mirror, two slides ahead).
4) Amber band — the provenance, with the portrait: Deming is the American quality pioneer whose cycle Toyota built its production system around; this room already runs PDCA on processes — now run it on prompts. The credential: the Lean Enterprise Institute (Deming/Toyota home turf) published “Prompt, Do, Check, Act: the new PDCA” in May 2026; their line — the people who get the most from these tools are the ones willing to run the loop a few more times. And every phase is delegable; the white lines show how.
5) At ACT/standardize, the Toyota phrase: standardized work — lock in the better way, then improve the standard (Part 6’s whole story). Anthropic’s golden rule, spoken: show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context — if they’d be confused, the model will be too.

BRIDGE —
“One clarification before the evidence — the two layers, on one worked prompt.”

ACRONYMS —
PDCA = Plan-Do-Check-Act — the Deming/Toyota improvement cycle, core of kaizen (continuous improvement).
gauge R&R = Gauge Repeatability & Reproducibility — a tested template kills prompt-to-prompt variation the way a calibrated gauge kills measurement variation.

YOU WRITE WITH THE ANATOMY · YOU IMPROVE WITH THE LOOP
Two layers, one craft
THE ANATOMY — design layer. What a prompt CONTAINS: the seven elements. Ask: is it complete?
THE LOOP — process layer. What you DO with it: Plan, Do, Check, Act. Ask: how does it get — and stay — good?
P
PLAN — the anatomy, all seven elements
Role: careful retail analyst — never invent numbers. Task: monthly returns report from the attached export. Context: columns = SKU · reason code · refund €. Format: one-page summary + top-5 table. Example: last month’s report, attached. The out: field missing → say so, don’t guess. The stop: deliver the report — nothing beyond.
D
DO — numbered sequence, wait-gates
1) Read the export; list the columns you actually see. 2) WAIT for my OK. 3) Build the table. 4) Draft the summary.
C
CHECK — named verification, stop-on-fail
Before showing me anything: reconcile the table to the export TOTAL. If it doesn’t reconcile, STOP and report the gap.
A
ACT — deliver the final output + improve
Deliver the final report. Then list what was ambiguous in this brief, so I can fix it for next month.
One brief, four sections — the loop written INTO the prompt: a wait-gate is a Do you kept; a stop-on-fail Check is a verification you refused to delegate.
In chat, you run the loop by hand. In agentic work, you write the loop into the brief — which is why it works best there. Part 5’s mission-brief template is exactly these four sections, grown up.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) The one-sentence thesis, verbatim: “You write with the anatomy — you improve with the loop.” Anatomy = what a prompt contains (design). PDCA = what you do with it (process). They are not rivals; they are layers.
2) Point at the blueprint: the schematic robot is the anatomy — a design you can inspect for completeness; the amber ring around it is the loop — the process that runs around ANY design, forever.
3) Walk the worked brief top to bottom, P → D → C → A. PLAN is simply the seven elements, filled, on a mundane monthly report. DO is the numbered sequence with the wait-gate. CHECK names a verification and STOPS on failure. ACT does BOTH of its jobs: deliver the final output, and name what to improve — the prompt asks for its own next revision.
4) The italic line under the brief: in agentic mode the loop lives INSIDE the prompt — a wait-gate is a Do you kept for yourself; a stop-on-fail Check is a verification you refused to delegate.
5) Close on the teal band, and tee Part 5: the mission brief is these four sections, grown up.

BRIDGE —
“Which of these methods survive scientific scrutiny — and which famous tricks don’t? The evidence corner.”

PDCA = Plan-Do-Check-Act (previous slide).
